definition: A fixed-size vector capturing voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks.
details: A fixed-size vector capturing voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks. Used for speaker verification, diarization, and as the conditioning signal in multi-speaker and cloned TTS.

explainer.lead: A speaker embedding such as an x-vector is a fixed-size vector that captures voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks. It matters because it turns voice identity into a compact signal usable across verification, diarization, and speech synthesis.

tiers.eli5: It is a short numeric fingerprint of a person's voice, so a computer can compare two voices by comparing their fingerprints.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use x-vectors for speaker verification and diarization, and as the conditioning signal in multi-speaker and cloned text-to-speech. A pitfall is that the same embedding can serve both identifying real speakers and conditioning cloned voices.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as a fixed-size vector capturing voice identity, trained on speaker-discrimination tasks. No formula or stated limits are given.

explainer.example: In a cloned TTS system, an x-vector extracted from a target voice is fed as the conditioning signal so the synthesizer produces speech in that voice.
